uncited: The method consists of two main phases: construction (building the structure from triangle data) and traversal (ray-grid intersection).
This article details the construction and data layout; traversal logic is covered in [Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal](6252-two-level-grid-ray-traversal.md).
**Top-Level Cells Array:** An array where each entry corresponds to a cell in the top-level grid.
**Leaf Array:** An array of intervals (start/end indices) into the Reference Array.
Each entry corresponds to a leaf cell (sub-grid cell) and stores two 32-bit integers: `start_index` and `end_index`.
These indices define the contiguous range in the Reference Array where primitives overlapping that specific leaf cell are stored.
**Reference Array:** A flat array storing pairs of `(leaf_cell_global_index, primitive_id)`.
Each primitive is referenced once for every leaf cell it overlaps.
References for the same leaf cell are stored contiguously.
The size of this array is determined during construction.
It builds the top-level grid first, then computes leaf cell locations, generates and sorts primitive-leaf pairs, and finally extracts the leaf intervals.
*   Compute the bounding box of all primitives: $b \leftarrow \text{COMPUTE BOUNDS}(t)$.
*   Compute the top-level grid resolution: $r \leftarrow \text{COMPUTE TOP LEVEL RESOLUTION}(b)$.
*   Upload triangle data to GPU memory: $t \leftarrow \text{UPLOAD TRIANGLES}(t)$.
*   Build a temporary uniform grid to initialize top-level cells: $\text{data} \leftarrow \text{BUILD UNIFORM GRID}(t, b, r)$.
This uses the sort-based approach by Kalojanov and Slusallek [KS09] to determine triangle-cell overlaps.
*   Get sorted top-level pairs (cell index, primitive ID): $\text{Atl}_p \leftarrow \text{GET SORTED TOP-LEVEL PAIRS}(\text{data})$.
*   Get the number of top-level references: $n \leftarrow \text{GET NUMBER OF TOP-LEVEL REFERENCES}(\text{data})$.
*   Get top-level cell ranges: $\text{tlc} \leftarrow \text{GET TOP-LEVEL CELL RANGES}(\text{data})$.
*   Initialize accumulator array $\text{Acc}$ of size $r_x \cdot r_y \cdot r_z + 1$ with zeros.
*   Count leaf cells per top-level cell: $\text{Acc} \leftarrow \text{COUNT LEAF CELLS}(b, r, \text{tlc})$.
This determines how many leaf cells each top-level cell will contain based on its resolution.
*   Perform exclusive scan on $\text{Acc}$: $\text{Acc} \leftarrow \text{EXCLUSIVE SCAN}(\text{Acc}, r_x \cdot r_y \cdot r_z + 1)$.
*   Initialize top-level cell ranges with scan results: $\text{tlc} \leftarrow \text{INITIALIZE}(\text{Acc}, \text{tlc})$.
This sets the `Location` field in the Top-Level Cells Array.
*   Initialize accumulator array $\text{Arc}$ of size $G_{ref} + 1$ (where $G_{ref}=128$) with zeros.

*   Count leaf references per top-level cell using a fast conservative triangle-cell intersection test (bounding box only): $\text{Arc} \leftarrow \text{COUNT LEAF REFS}(t, b, r, n, \text{Atl}_p, \text{tlc})$.
*   Perform exclusive scan on $\text{Arc}$: $\text{Arc} \leftarrow \text{EXCLUSIVE SCAN}(\text{Arc}, G_{ref} + 1)$.
*   Get total size $m \leftarrow \text{Arc}[G_{ref}]$.
*   Allocate leaf pairs array $\text{Ap}$ of size $m$.
*   Write pairs $(\text{Leaf Location}, \text{Primitive ID})$ to $\text{Ap}$.
*   **Leaf Location Key:** The global memory location in the leaf array is used as the key.
This is computed from the leaf index relative to the top-level cell and the location of the first leaf for that top-level cell (from $\text{tlc}$).
*   **Intersection Test:** Use a more precise test (including plane intersection) when generating the pairs.
*   $\text{Ap} \leftarrow \text{WRITE PAIRS}(t, b, r, n, \text{Atl}_p, \text{tlc}, \text{Arc})$.
*   Sort $\text{Ap}$ using an improved radix sort by Billeter et al. [BOA09] with two- and four-way splits.
*   $\text{Ap} \leftarrow \text{SORT}(\text{Ap})$.
*   Extract cell ranges from the sorted reference array to finalize leaf cell intervals.
Check for range borders (neighboring pairs with different keys) to determine start and end indices for each leaf cell.
*   $\text{leaves} \leftarrow \text{EXTRACT CELL RANGES}(\text{Ap}, m)$.

The source explicitly describes the structure as a 'fixed depth hierarchy' (two-level) with a 'sparse top-level grid' containing sub-grids (leaf grids) of 'arbitrary resolution'. It contrasts this with uniform grids (referencing the 'teapot in a stadium problem') which suffer in sparse regions, implying the two-level grid consumes less memory or provides better efficiency for non-uniform distributions compared to a single high-resolution uniform grid. The construction algorithm is described as 'sort-based' (using radix sort) and implemented in CUDA, which is optimized for parallel GPU execution. The claim's comparison to '[Multi-Level Array Grid]' is contextual; the evidence supports the specific technical details of the method described (fixed two-level, sort-based, GPU-optimized, variable resolution sub-grids) as being distinct from complex linked structures or varying depths found in other hierarchical methods, and specifically notes the memory/efficiency benefits over uniform grids.
